I think the readers of NYTimes deserve a better article than offered by these two economists who engage in hand wringing over the coming future of too few people to populate their economic models.  They offer few numbers in their analysis.  The numbers are largely confined to birth rates that confirm the reduced population they predict.
   They do not define the population curve that is ideal, according to their model, to perpetuate a healthy economy.   This is a failing of their analysis.
   A population that expands at historic rates - doubling from 2.5 billion in 1950 to 5 billion in1987 (37 years) and adding another 3 billion by 2022 (35 years) cannot be sustained.  So, what is their solution if catastrophic population increase is ruled out?
   Let me quote - "Smaller water systems spend more money per gallon and deliver dirtier water," and contrast that statement with the understanding that water supplies worldwide are in crisis.  To the likely rejoinder that technology will find a solution, I respond that I can use that same argument to dismiss the authors' arguments about a coming disaster.
   I question the motivation of the authors when they state "There are many billions of lives that could be good — many as good as your life, many better — that will not be lived in a depopulating future."  This seems, at best, a religious statement, not an economic statement.

comments.name: leave_it_to_me
comments.body: What a great article. It began with a personal journey and evolved into a history of  how the disabled are treated by the public and by the government. I've had a rare illness for my entire life. It wasn't diagnosed until I was nearly 30 years old, followed by another rare disease. It can't be seen although it causes pain and limits what I can and can't do. This article caught my attention because a couple of months ago I had an accident and injured my left knee. Strangely, this injury from which I will recover (that's the plan) has produced sympathy whereas the hidden disability is treated as an "all in my head" affliction.  Before the ACA every medical insurance change resulted in a exclusion. My current insurance wants me to have useless tests that are uncomfortable, redundant and a waste of time. The way I handled this was to specialize my teaching to empathy -for children, animals, and people in general. The focus was on saving the planet together. I received a teaching degree and a specialized certification. I did not share with my child and adult audiences that I had a disability because that was not the point and frankly, I would have lost my job thanks to the female version of Trump that ran the organization.  My disability is no longer a secret but I've experienced people that would not hug me, a person that called the police when I parked in the handicapped spot and more. As I age I find less sympathy.

Before my mother died, age 100, she went from pretty totally ambulatory (even after a spiral femur fracture) to cautious, to holding onto another person, to cane, to walker. She didn't like not being able to stride along, but she was happy to be upright and progressing on her local sidewalks.

Those sidewalks contained ramps at the corners, and one day she commented, "Isn't it nice of the restaurants and shops to install these ramps for those of us with walkers and even people with baby strollers?"

I explained that the ramps were provided in compliance with the ADA. She claimed she had never heard of the ADA, and was a bit disgruntled -- that I had destroyed her fantasy of kind retailers and restauranteurs!

However, she used those ramps for several more years.

At some point in our lives, each of us will be more or less disabled. That means that people walking along, no worries, are *temporarily able*.

I was a runner and my orthopedist told me that I would never run much again. He was right--for 6 months. Then I found a PT who specialized in back issues. It's been 11 years, I run over 1,000 miles a year, much of it on trails. I do 30K to 25-mile trail races in the mountains around Bozeman, MT; I backpack, ski and mountain bike. Thus far his year I've climbed over 260,000 vertical feet, a typical stat for me. PT has become my religion--2 or more hours per week of stretching and strengthening often supplemented by weightlifting. 

My back issues are specific to me. I'm sure what I've been trained to do by a legion of physical therapists who regularly adjust my regimen in response to new issues, won't work for everyone; as this article indicates, the sources of back pain are myriad. But with dedication, I am able to live the life I choose, pushing myself harder than all but a few people my age, and I am mostly pain free. You can find me at RagingWhileAging.com.

The beauty of capitalism is its ability to change and adapt to varying circumstances.  Did Apple experience a downturn when Steve Jobs died?  No, it flourished under Tim Cook.

comments.name: CA_LaLaLand
comments.body: Jensen Huang is the key person responsible for creating and perpetuating the AI bubble—propping up the entire stock market. At least for now.

articles.title: Why the U.S. Can’t Afford to Let Nvidia Fail
articles.summary: The Opinion contributing writer Natasha Sarin explains why the chip maker — and its leader Jensen Huang — are so important to the A.I. industry as a whole.

comments.name: Ken
comments.body: Trump and his Administration have reached unprecedented and unbearable levels of government corruption, flouting of law and undermining of America's vital national security interests. When the new Congress convenes, there should be a bipartisan moral obligation to impeach Trump immediately before he can do more damage to America's institutions and standing on the world's stage. The case against Trump speaks for itself (in legal terms "res ipsa loquitur").

comments.name: Steve
comments.body: Forget the investigatuons, comittees and internal wrangling. Jack Smith's report plus the current overwhelming public opinion  is already enough to impeach Trump and beware any politician who votes against it.

comments.name: Tom J,
comments.body: There is absolutely nothing to be gained by conducting a 3rd impeachment, whether or not it's deserved.  First, Trump would never be convicted in the Senate.  Second, it's a moot point.  In two years he will be out of politics.  Third, it would be a terrible waste of time and do nothing for Democrats to honor their campaign promises related to affordability, housing, homelessness, etc. We have severe problems with the national debt, funding social security, the implementaion of data centers and AI.  Democrats need to stay focused on those issues and on their campaign promises and not on futile impeachments and investigations.  The last election was a mandate for Democrats to fix real problems, not waste time.  Republicans had a mandate when Trump was elected and proceeded to waste their advantage by not addressing the needs of voters.  Democrats better have learned a lesson from that or they'll be ousted next time.

comments.name: Serban
comments.body: One way or another Trump & co. staggering corruption cannot go unpunished. If it does it signals that the law does not exist for the powerful and the US is no better than countries were rulers grab everything they can.

comments.name: John
comments.body: The problem hasn't been recognized.  There is no "revered" position or station to  be corrupted. The sad fact that humans apparently need such designated status is the problem.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: The voters dealt with the corruption by electing dems. Take the low hanging fruit like hegseth and Kennedy but forget the endless senate hearings and just govern. People want healthcare, financial security, real solutions for the border,  and yes lower gas prices. They want decency to be restored.

comments.name: EJS
comments.body: I would like to see the Democrats in Congress pass a series of one-issue laws: 1. Lift the ceiling on the social security tax, securing its financing for decades; 2. Restore the Affordable Care Act subsidies; 3. Raise the federal minimum wage; 4. End the financing of the war against Iran; 5. Abolish the carried interest tax scam for hedge fund managers; 6. Prohibit members of Congress from engaging in stock trading. Do all that, then go on to other issues and consider impeachment, first, of members of Trump's cabinet.

comments.name: Midwesterner
comments.body: Democrats must prioritize the policies that will help Americans with affordability, healthcare, education, childcare, housing, and all the other issues that impact us daily. While I would also love to see Trump held accountable for his many crimes, if the Democrats pursue investigations at the expense of policy, they will waste an opportunity. Even if they come up with an easy-to-follow narrative like corruption, they still likely won't have the votes in the Senate to convict Trump. So, yes, proceed with the investigations--and prepare to continue them into 2028 and beyond--but let's prioritize policy.

articles.title: Common Grounds for Impeachment
articles.summary: What should House Democrats focus on? There is so much to choose from.

comments.name: Tommy
comments.body:
If any of us plebes had engaged with a possible Chinese spy or manipulated the market, the charges would be filed in a minute. 

Almost every day, this guy pushes past boundaries the limits of which we thought had been reached.

comments.name: Steven
comments.body: If an issue has consequences for everyone else then it's important. But if it's consequences for the ultra wealthy then no matter how important the issue seemed before, now it's unimportant. Once you place everything into this lens you'll see how it works, from infidelity to insider trading, from national security to child abuse. They've bought their way out of consequences and if you're not ultra wealthy you're not a spectator, you're a player who has to actually follow the rules.

comments.name: CleoCatra
comments.body: It's one thing for the government to regulate businesses in general terms; it's entirely another for an administration to be personally invested/intertwined in the day-to-day management of a particular company and the fate of its CEO. The economic health and national security of a democratic country should not depend on what happens with a single business or individual. That ought to go without saying.

comments.name: Ben
comments.body: This story is more than just about Nvidia. Together with how the market was rigged for SpaceX’s IPO, it shows that the entire American stock market has been sold out to billionaires. This has several major implications: There can be no trust in existing market checks and balances. Combined with how Trumps and the GOP destroyed the government’s checks and balances, America is full on in authoritarian oligarchy territory now. It also means Americans’ pension funds’ investments, the people’s largest, private safety net, is not safe at all. The wealth of individuals is riskier now than it was after the Enron scandal and the Great Recession of 2008. It also shows the devaluation of honesty and serious moral decay in America today, and how success in the stock market not just doesn’t represent reality for everyday Americans, it’s inversely related to their wellbeing.

comments.name: AhBrightWings
comments.body: Again explain to me how this is not a flagrant crime. Trump's family clearly bought in the trough and made millions (billions?) in days. This is an outrageous example of insider trading, among other things.

comments.name: SG
comments.body: Where are the consequences? When will Trump face consequences for clear market manipulation?

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: Once again, we see that rules and laws only apply to some of us. If you are rich and powerful enough, you get to do whatever you want. No society can function like this in the long run. A reckoning is coming one way or another.

comments.name: SanFranciscoReader
comments.body: A new front in economic intervention?  How about a continuation of the same kinds of economic interventions on his own behalf that the current president has been making since the beginning of his first term?

articles.title: Trump’s Nvidia Move Heralds a New Front in Economic Intervention
articles.summary: Presidents before him have bailed out companies in times of national crisis. Mr. Trump went further: He staked the fortunes of the United States on those of a favored chief executive.

comments.name: Tintin
comments.body: There's a larger issue here that needs to be discussed more openly and more often: We're sick of CEOs. The grotesque pay disparities, the entitlement, the greed, the disregard for other people's interests. We're tired of them. It's time to make CEOs look like the pariahs they are.  Whether it's Elizabeth Holmes or Steve Jobs, the weird level of greed among these people is finally, finally excessive enough that they deserve our open disdain.  The fact that Trump appears to be caught in the past when CEOs garnered influence is all the more reason to deplore them now.

comments.name: demonut
comments.body: Follow the money.... I wonder who made money by buying Nvidia stock last week after it had declined by 47% and selling it today on its recovery? Interesting to check out stock trading of people around Trump who could have been fed inside information about Huang's reinstatement.

comments.name: Old Badger
comments.body: Really. Our challenge to keep democracy is going to be the billionaires vs the working class. Think French Revolution.

comments.name: undisclosed
comments.body: trump was merely protecting HIS investment. period.

comments.name: PVR
comments.body: After a total of 6 years of Trump "shooting people on 5th Avenue" the republicans in congress has finally decided he needs a little bit of oversight.  Had the GOP not gotten spanked in the midterms, they would still be shirking their constitutional duties.   But give them a few weeks and their righteous indignation will evaporate - just like it did after Jan 6.  Every republican who held congressional office while Trump was robbing Americans blind should be voted out at the earliest possible opportunity.

comments.name: Publius II
comments.body:
Who owns who—does Trump own Huang or Huang own Trump?  This is the way the French nobility acted before the French Revolution and you know what happened to them. 

An overwhelming majority think Trump is corrupt—this may increase that majority to 95%.  

Will this be the straw that breaks Trump’s back—impeachment and conviction?  His every act seems to bring him closer to being fired.

comments.name: Maple09
comments.body:
I wonder how Amica's closest allies, especially members of the Five Eyes, feel about sharing intelligence with the Trump Regime these days. Meanwhile Trump constantly denigrates most of America's allies while threatening them and harming their economies.
Does this make Americans feel safe. Or are they oblivious to the risks?

comments.name: Unconventional Liberal
comments.body:
Shame on the Nvidia Board of Directors.
Huang violated his own company's policies on relationships.
He failed to resist a Chinese "honey pot" spy operation.
He lied to the Board of Directors when asked about Alice Huang.
Everyone will look at him differently from now on.
He has his job back for the moment. 
I'm not sure he'll keep it. He shouldn't.

articles.title: When You’re a Star They Let You Compromise National Security
articles.summary: Huang’s firing damaged something Donald Trump values even more than national security: the stock market.

comments.name: Cai
comments.body: I'm not sure people recognize what an awkward position Canada is in.  Trump would likely flip out if we declared the U.S. not a safe country.  Also, if we did so, Trump could "solve" his immigration issues by simply pushing everyone ICE detained to the Canadian border.  He might think "Why worry about deporting people, it's easy if you just line em up on the Ambassador bridge and push.  After all, Canada owes us bigly for freeloading...". Our population base is not that big.  We take in a greater percentage of immigrants, but there is a risk that too high a limit, or no limit, would lead to backlash.  People here are worried about Trump trying to destroy our auto and steel industries.  Cost of living concerns are also a big deal here.  Immigrants to Canada tend to remain in a few cities, for at least a decade.  Toronto has very high rents already.  Actually, you need to be about 2 hours away before they fall significantly.  I believe there is an effort to pass a law allowing more immigration, if immigrants agree to live in other areas of the country.  We are dealing with the same ageing demographic, we know we need more working age people.  Basically, we are trying to be humane without triggering overreaction that would end up making the situation worse.

comments.name: Simon
comments.body: I hate trump as much as the next guy, but for all the talk about current US immigration policy cruelty and hatefulness, I must point out that no nation on Earth has been more open to immigration. Even the progressive Nordic countries have been more rigorous in enforcing their immigration laws and insisting on full assimilation. Much of the alleged “cruelty” we see in current policies would have been unnecessary if we had properly enforced laws and thoroughly vetted all immigrants before opening the door. I am not surprise that Canada is taking a US-like approach to this issue.

comments.name: Steffie
comments.body: I fully understand the predicament the Canadian government faces, given its fraught relationship with the current US administration. However, to use the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement to bar Haitians who, in essence, are being hunted down by the Immigration & Customs Enforcement (ICE) agency is absurd. Even US citizens, White ones to boot, are not safe under this regime (the names of the late Ms. Good and the late Mr. Pretti come to mind). Various Canadian human rights organizations, including Amnesty International Canada, have urged the Canadian government to withdraw from the treaty: https://thelinknewspaper.ca/article/refugee-advocates-renew-calls-for-canada-to-withdraw-from-u.s-border-agreement. Like many people around the world, I hold the Canadian Prime Minister, Mr. Mark Carney, in high regard, and hope he and his government will, at a minimum, suspend the agreement with the United States until such time that unauthorized aliens in the US will have the opportunity to state their case in a US court.

comments.name: GSL
comments.body: I take no joy in saying this, but I guess Canada can stop throwing stones. Glass houses, and all.

comments.name: DF
comments.body: What is weird about this is the lack of waiver for a spouse into Canada.  Their rules stated you needed a relative.  Just because she's not a blood relative, she's a no-go.  She's married and her husband and children are related to a Canadian legal resident (or citizen).  Why would they separate out a spouse. To me an in-law is a relative.  For those of you thinking you can 'escape' to Canada when things get 'really bad'.  Think again.

comments.name: N Ba
comments.body: They could all live together without worrying about US or Canadian immigration policy if they all returned to Haiti.

comments.name: Ned
comments.body: About a billion people live in “rich” countries, where many, as we know, are poor. Two more billion live in middle or upper middle income counties. The remaining five billion live in poor countries, more often than not ridden with crime and extreme corruption. Given the chance 90% of the people in the last group will move to the first group. This is understandable as every one knows that he/she has only one life and wants to make it better. But there is simply no place for the people from the third group in the countries from the first group. And not anyone, regardless how progressive he/she is, has called “abolish all borders!”

comments.name: simon
comments.body: I love Canada, but am very disappointed in this policy.It is heartless.

articles.title: Families Fleeing the U.S. Are Being Separated at the Canadian Border
articles.summary: Driven to Canada by deportation fears, some members of Haitian families are being denied entry, turned back and detained by U.S. authorities.

comments.name: Mark McIntyre
comments.body:
Financial markets have a mind of their own but most of these AI startups are not profitable and building data centers on borrowed money. Much of that lending is coming from Mr. Huang.

Wall St., after much irrational exuberance, is finally asking where are the revenue streams and profits going to come from to justify these astronomical valuations? Markets don't seem to like what they're seeing.

comments.name: Steve Ell
comments.body:
Jensen Huang’s return is not ok.

Politicians shouldn’t be involved in corporate governance.
Government shouldn’t own stocks, except in special cases like the automotive bailouts years ago.
The entire board should be replaced.

Huang has lost my respect. Infidelity is a human fault. Getting involved with an agent of an adversary government should have been prevented. Doesn’t Huang have a security team? Shouldn’t they have prevented this?

trump knew months ago that something nefarious was afoot. he abetted the situation by his inaction. lutnick is also involved and he or his business or his sons are reaping the benefits. It’s interesting that Cantor Fitzgerald held on to more than one million shares after selling two thirds of its holdings, but more recently established a position of 1.3 million put options as of 9/30/26 according to public filings - Form 13F.

As a result, they benefit regardless of the direction the stock moves. Why now? Why not last year. Something stinks.

The scandal has not ended. There’s going to be more negative consequences before it does.

comments.name: Lisa
comments.body: “The markets” need to continue to slide.  It’s the only hope of a soft landing to this bursting bubble.

comments.name: kcbob
comments.body:
The markets are wary.  Sharper investors know Mr Huang is not likely to survive this.  

He will need to go before committees in both the House and Senate - probably before the Democrats take over.   Both he and Trump may have committed treason.  The board members may also be culpable.

The chips transferred to China ended up in the hands of their military, adding to the danger for our members of the Armed Forces.  

Even Republicans in Congress are genuinely outraged.  They feel betrayed.

The Invidia scandal is not going away.  It may prove the 'smoking gun' that pushes Republicans over the edge in impeachment.  After Congress changes hands, only one-in-four of the remaining 44 Republicans needs to vote to convict for a guilty verdict.

The bar will get lower the longer this goes on.

comments.name: Sassy
comments.body: What’s the therapeutic protocol for sharing secrets with spies?

comments.name: JCarmel
comments.body: Just when you thought this president and his administration could not be more nakedly corrupt…

comments.name: Judi T
comments.body: OOPS! If Huang isn’t a “tech bro” or “above the law”, and Trump told an “untruth” about having anything to do with Huang’s reinstatement, Jensen probably just lost his title of “Great Patriot and National Treasure.” That’s probably why NVidia stock went down again today.

comments.name: F S
comments.body: Intervention from a convicted felon, several times bankrupt businessman and named many times in the Epstein files.... sound economics judgment.

articles.title: Markets Slide as Tech Stocks Partly Reverse Nvidia-Sparked Rally
articles.summary: Shares have veered wildly for days, pushed and pulled by the drama at Nvidia and the rise and fall of Anthropic’s stock after its blockbuster public offering.

comments.name: Paula
comments.body:
The majority of the disparaging reviews are so similar, 
I can't help but wonder if a PR firm was engaged - 
similar to the one hired to trash Blake Lively.
By whom, I'm not sure.

comments.name: Marcia
comments.body:
The entire royal family needs to go.
There main duties are cutting ribbons on new shopping centers, community centers, clinics and hospitals. Oh, and waving to crowds.
They should each pick one tiara and one royal residence, give the rest back to the state and go live their lives.
They and Britain have become a joke.

comments.name: Fomo brood
comments.body: They just are no different than Trump in many ways. Banking on their name to make some money, any way possible. People criticize Ms Trump but Meghan is no different. Milking the name for every last pound.  Its why I  really hate royals of any kind. They think they are better than anyone else. They lead a very privileged life often with  lots of tax breaks or no tax like the Dutch royal family . We even pay for the upkeep of their palaces and yachts and they pay ZERO tax. Even the kids get money , like 2 million+.  Yeah I am sure their life  is very hard. Viva the  republic.

comments.name: Hello
comments.body: No fan of Meghan, she's so self-satisfied, which is hard to like. But, actually, most of all, I think she's dim. What else explains so many unnecessary mistakes and decisions, creating her problems with the public? Whatever racism exists is horrific and, for that, she deserves sympathy. But the rest is on her for bringing around so much ire.

comments.name: An Independent
comments.body: This reminds me of those horrible group projects in college where one or a couple people parasitically milk everyone else’s conscientiousness and end up with the same grade. Instead of enduring the countless planning meetings, library research, paper drafts, rework, final paper, audiovisuals, note cards for the presentation, etc., some people instead just show up for the presentation and schmooze their way through it and get an equal grade and equal credit.

comments.name: Anon
comments.body: I’m glad they are back in the UK so that their kids aren’t deprived of their cultural inheritance.  But really, those two need to apologize for betraying the royal family and then pipe down.  The rest of the family can’t risk letting them get close again and that’s so sad for the kids.  But they won’t because they have shockingly bad judgment.

comments.name: Allen Carney
comments.body: What these comments reflect is that no matter what the opinions, these royals and "non-royals" are impossible to ignore and generate curious emotional and often bizarre fascination.

comments.name: Hamid Varzi
comments.body: How can this entitled couple demand any respect when they dragged the royal family through the mud? Their hypocrisy in demanding privacy was exposed by their constant search for publicity. They can't have it both ways.

articles.title: ‘Nonroyal Royals’: How Harry and Meghan Are Settling Back Into Britain
articles.summary: Six years after leaving the country, the Sussexes are back and arranging a careful program of public appearances. Will they complement the royal family, or compete with it?

comments.name: David W.
comments.body:
I wonder what might happen if a neighbour decided to adopt the principle, I am old, single, no longer working, I don't need such a big house on such a big property, so close to the city, perhaps I will knock it down and put up a small apartment building and take one of the apartments and allow 4 or 5 other families to live closer to the city and the ravine in my backyard.

I wonder would Mr. Ruck join with the neighbours  when they point out the bylaws that would prevent such a common sense thing from happening.

comments.name: Will
comments.body: Hooray Wolf Ruck! In the last few years, more lawns are going "native." You see it in LA. In London, where we live now, we planted a small English meadow to replace boring turf. I counted 26 species of wildflower and grass! The joint was hoppin, buzzing with bees. After we moved out the landlord mowed it down, dug it up and returned it to grass  Sigh. A wild natural garden is SO MUCH more interesting, and beautiful, and easy. We will get there.

comments.name: M
comments.body:
I love this article. It gives me hope. I live in an apartment complex. They don't use pesticides. 
More articles like this please.

comments.name: David
comments.body: I delight in the fact that I haven't had a lawn in 35 years.  Especially since my chore growing up was mowing the lawn.

comments.name: Jim
comments.body: Good luck Wolf man. I live in the woods- could never tolerate your neighbors or that noise, all their absurd behaviors in their little yards where they reenact all the primordial things that they have lost as a now urban, industrial species. If more people were willing to fight against that thoughtlessness, perhaps less of it would exist. So, thank you. Also, always nice to hear when Canadians also do some of the moronic things Americans do.

comments.name: ayc
comments.body: Thank you for your deeply moving reporting on one man's effort to expand the amount of nature in place of the lawn.  Americans are brought up to worship impeccably maintained lawns the way Trump worships performative masculinity.  The industrial complex and the billion-dollar industry are worthy incentives to keep this obsession going.  I am rooting for Wolf and the movement that aligns with what he is doing.  In the HOA community I live in, I will be fined if my lawn is not well kept.  HOA can also forcibly spend my money to do whatever it takes if my lawn falls below the community standard, so that the property value is not compromised.

comments.name: David Michael Rogers
comments.body: Irony is the fifth fundamental force of the universe. (Ms. "Earthy") And now she's famous for defending lawn care. Probably not her finest hour. Glad Mr. Wolf prevailed.

comments.name: Anna
comments.body: You can have both some lawn, grown without chemicals, plus areas of locally native plants to support wildlife esp birds and the insects they need to live.  A baby bird eats 1,000 bugs before it leaves the nest.  One key element is to leave the fall leaves that fall in your garden beds, as that’s where butterflies, lightning bugs etc spend the winter, and don’t use blowers or chemicals.

articles.title: His Lawn Grows Wild. Trouble Follows.
articles.summary: This is the story of an Olympic canoeist and one very controversial lawn.

comments.name: Mary Sweeney
comments.body: As a consumer I do not want to buy food contaminated with lead. I also do not want to buy food from Texas where they are planning to spread fracking waste on farmland. We need immediate legislation to stop these practices or, at the very least, to put warning labels on food grown in these and other poisoned areas. I realize that innocent farmers would be harmed by such labels but they should be compensated by the responsible party whether that is the U.S. Army or a private fracking disposal firm. Maybe if polluters had to compensate those who are harmed these dangerous practices would stop. As it is now the public pays with serious health problems and entire ecosystems suffer as well.

comments.name: cmk
comments.body: The gravity with which these people speak would be a lot more believable if it had been applied to a non-explosive solution back in March.  Or, for that matter, in '25 when they discovered the conditions.

comments.name: Jay
comments.body: This deterioration cannot have come as a surprise to the Army. Why this was not anticipated and planned for years ago is inexcusable. The Arm's failure to do so is what is creating a potential health risk for those in communities surrounding the blast site. What arrangements has the Army made to help people who may suffer from the effects of this blast? Or did they not anticipate that either? Do they think that telling people to 'hide under their desks and cover their heads' is enough to absolve them of any responsibility? Again: this is inexcusable.

comments.name: Val
comments.body:
It is amazing how much people can try to biohack their lives in 2026, but we also have a more lackadaisical attitude with environmental exposure, such as this new comfortability with lead exposure. I wonder what our environment and health would look like if people stopped hyperfocusing on the little they can control with doing things like counting their macros and instead focused on these larger systems.

I guess MAHA really wants to go back to the good old days with things like leaded gasoline.

comments.name: Ian
comments.body: Is the Army going to pay for ongoing routine testing for lead exposure for the public affected? Who will be held accountable?

comments.name: Andy
comments.body:
I did see a man though, on one interview who lived nearly against the fence. 
On account of most places on earth, and especially Jassenova, I say let him stay, and let these failing things go away. 
My own father went insane because his hip broke and it was made of cobalt (and it was actually sold by my stepfather to the hospital in question!) so I can say he's still safe. But if he goes crazy over this lead drift in question, here I stage my qualms.

.... - -  As IF we don't have a way to clean their drywall by now.

comments.name: Pete Fisher
comments.body: Republican office holders, historically, don't worry about lead exposure and its horrible effects. They were in charge and made the decisions that allowed the Flint Michigan Lead exposure catastrophe to occur.  Also in February 2026 this Republican Congress voted to cut $125 million from Lead-pipe replacement funding under the 2021 infrastructure law.  Republican office holders don't seem to worry about Lead exposure to their constituents, no matter how it happens.

comments.name: Kate J
comments.body: I used to work in our state Environmental Quality Agency, and learned a few things about lead exposure. People younger than I am should have much lower blood lead levels than someone my age (71), due partly to the use of leaded gasoline and paint containing lead in the past, and of course stopping that kind of use when the harm was recognized. As I recall, my blood lead level was roughly 4 when tested. The important thing to recognize that blood lead levels should be zero!  As the article says, there are no safe exposures, no natural amounts of lead in humans or other animals. It's shocking to me that this mass exposure is about to happen largely due to incompetent "planning"

articles.byline: Evan Halper, Quinn Glabicki and Hiroko Tabuchi

comments.name: Anon
comments.body:
Evidence is strongly on the side of significant genetic influence on personality, temperment, and intelligence.

Common sense and the extremely obvious experience of most human beings is as well.

Anyone who has made it their mission to disprove what is both scientifically supported and obvious to most people is an ideologue with an axe to grind. Beware.

Concern about the effect on society seem silly, when I think the overwhelming majority of people already operate on the assumption that our personalities and intelligence are significantly heritable and intractable. Maybe some of our educational institutions don't operate on this assumption, but it is hard to see what they would do differently except increase tracking and vocational programs, which would be wonderful, because they would bring education in line with real needs and result in kids getting more appropriate preparation for their adult lives.

Also, women need to think of the way the idea that "parenting is everything" can lead to deeply oppressive and misogynist parenting cultures, like "gentle parenting" and other forms of helicoptering that fall on women.

comments.name: George S
comments.body: A view of history, at least to me, suggests that nurture is far more determinative. Yesterday's Vikings who gave words like slaughter, ransack, and anger are today's bike-riding, unversal healthcare-dealing, Nobel Prize-awarding pacificists. Yesterday's Mongols, who introduced the world to biological warfare and made an art of mass sexual violence as they swept across Eurasia, are today's most agreeable herders. Genetically, these are largely the same people. The environments that nutured them changed. Climate change and population growth pushed what had been peaceful people to expand far and wide. Scandinavians and Mongols aren't genetically more violent than other people. How they were nutured changed. Similarly, while there are some differences in cognitive ability at birth, we have evidence that the environment a child grows in is far more determinative of future outcomes in cognition and learning than genetics. On the bright side, the vast majority of us are born with the cognitive tools to be quite intelligent adults. In a darker view, the vast majority of us are also born with the cognitive tools to toss diseased corpses over the walls of a city we are seiging and planning to raise to the soil after killing all of its men and boys and enslaving its women and girls. We contain multitudes.

comments.name: Bobby
comments.body: This will never be resolved until we conduct proper scientific testing and observation on people.

comments.name: Gene Henry
comments.body: Referencing Bruni's essay today, "the apple does not fall far from the tree."

comments.name: Calvin Hobbes
comments.body:
“… an uncomfortable frontier in a culture anchored in the egalitarian promise that, through sheer will and circumstance, anyone can become anything.”

If mom and dad are both short and unathletic, can their son through sheer will and circumstance (whatever that is) become an NBA center?

If mom and dad both grew up in typical American school districts and were high school dropouts or barely graduated from high school, can their child through sheer will and circumstance win a Nobel Prize in Physics?

No.

comments.name: DJS
comments.body:
“If  cognitive ability is intrinsic... “

“If ?! “  

“..what does that mean for federal learning programs designed to level the playing field, like Head Start? “

It doesn’t mean anything. Those programs provide enrichment.
No program can level the playing field.  The same children who were at the top of my class in kindergarten were at the top of the class in high school.No amount of remedial education leveled the playing field as intelligence is inborn.  The student body was homogenous.

Everyone doesn’t start with the same blank slate.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
How does a digital system become "out of date?"  What and why makes that happen?

My automobile, sitting outside in the weather at all times and driving over bumpy roads, takes a beating.  Eventually it wears out and must be scrapped.  But my computer doesn't move and suffers no physical wear.  Yet my car lasts twice as long as the computer.

When my computer becomes "out of date" it is because the tech industry has chosen to make it so.  I had a perfectly fine old computer that stopped working because the software would no longer work on the internet or with other software. The software companies upgraded their products with no backward compatibility. 

Note that in the mainframe world, old software keeps running for decades. My employer runs 40 year programs.  Indeed, IBM maintained compatibility for its older machines for decades. Some users never bothered to upgrade their old programs, they continued to work just fine as written.

In contrast, the modern personal computer - internet world constantly upgrades even when there's no valid reason to do so.  Well, it does force customers to buy new hardware and software to keep up, so they make fresh sales.

As to vulnerabilities, back in 1980 computer hacking was well known.  They made movies and TV shows about it (e.g. "War Games"). So, they had 40 years to fix things.  Why haven't they? Why are computers so unnecessarily complicated?  Why are they so tightly tied together so that failures cascade?

comments.name: Joel Fritz
comments.body: I'm a programmer who retired in 2010.  I worked in the corporate office of a specialty retailer.  Like most people in business IT I was concerned about security.  There's a truism in programming that any large scale software system, whether it's an operating system or applications, is vulnerable to attack.  Another factor is that humans, including cybercriminals are ingenious.  Technology often makes fraud easier.  The cost of mail fraud dropped by a huge amount when email and text messaging became the norm.  Using the mail required paying postage, buying stationery, and getting the messages prepared and distributed.  AI is a greater step forward for fraud.  Computers are much better at brute force than humans.  Because they can gather and process data much faster than wetware they're ideal tools for the sort of trial and error involved in searching for software vulnerabilities.  Add large scale machines and self modifying code to the mix and you get a wonderful tool.  There is one constant.  Software will always have bugs.  The battle between cybersecurity people and cyberfraud people will continue to be a Spy vs. Spy thing.  Both sides will improve their tools.

comments.name: Michael Levy
comments.body: In the late 1980s I had a brief due in the Third Circuit Court of Appeals. It was just over 50 pages long. I edited it with a careful eye, but it was still over the 50-page limit. It was the beginning of modern word processing. (WordPerfect 4.2). I shrunk all the margins by a tiny bit and reduced the font from 12 point to 11.9. That did it. The Court of Appeals eventually figured out how to deal with this. The Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure specify the minimum font size and allow exceeding the page limit only if the word count is less than a designated maximum. The rule requires the attorney to sign it, and it "must include a certificate by the attorney, or an unrepresented party, that the document complies with the type-volume limitation. The person preparing the certificate may rely on the word or line count of the word-processing system used to prepare the document. The certificate must state the number of words--or the number of lines of monospaced type--in the document."

Four findings deserve far more attention than they receive.
First, Hispanic Americans outlive white Americans by nearly three years, despite substantial economic disadvantages and barriers to healthcare. Any serious explanation of racial health disparities must account for this apparent paradox.
Second, the narrowing Black-white mortality gap is heavily concentrated in three areas: cancer, HIV and heart disease, which together account for 68 percent of the convergence among men and 53 percent among women. This suggests that specific medical breakthroughs, pharmaceutical innovations and behavioral changes may explain much of the progress rather than a broad reduction in racial inequality.
Third, rising white mortality from certain causes, including suicide, also contributed to the convergence. 
Fourth, some disparities have proved remarkably resistant to improvement. The persistence or worsening of disparities involving homicide, maternal mortality, strokes and kidney disease demands closer scrutiny. 
Effective public policy requires identifying the specific mechanisms behind both progress and persistent inequality.

The complexity of the human experience is only very recently beginning to be understood.  By that I mean, of course, the tip if the iceberg with at least 2/3 left to be discovered.

A simple example is depression.  Is it emotional and psychological?  Is it physiological?  Is it related to life experiences, traumatic brain injury, toxic exposure, poor nutrition, toxic relationships, gut microbiome, etc., etc.?  Likely all of the above and more.  The growing field of functional medicine is beginning to untangle these many threads and one of the challenges is how to assess for all of these possibilities, is there a roadmap of likely candidates for each presenting constellation of symptoms and do we have effective interventions beyond drug therapy to address causal factors rather than treating the symptoms one at a time?  I'm hopeful that when the current raft of anti-science troglodytes is swept away, we will make progress in these endeavors.

But something about Bush being re-elected made me rethink my entire moral code and the purpose of life. It’s hard to explain. All I know is that I started walking furiously uptown on Broadway. I don’t know why. I kept walking and eventually found myself at 72nd st. I went into Gray’s Papaya and ordered a hot dog. I then ate the first meat I had eaten since the Carter administration. My intention was to get sick and purge myself of the poison of being the citizen of a country that would re-elect this man.

I did not get sick. After I ate that Gray’s Papaya hot dog I felt a sudden surge of energy. I felt better than I had in decades. I flew up staircases.

Experts and think tanks in the industry had already distilled how Biden’s export restrictions helped China’s chips industry. They diverted investment from Nvidia’s chips because of those restrictions toward building their own. The U.S had been selling chips to China for years before those restrictions. China was 5-10 years behind because of that dependency. Now because of these restrictions, China has stated its urgency in becoming independent of the U.S., building their own moat, and taking our market share because of this drama. What happens when they build a chip that is 80% as fast and half as expensive? We’re looking to curb their AI models with export restrictions, which are only 6 months behind anyway, at the risk of losing our global dominance in the chips market long-term. The U.S. is looking at the worst fumble in economic and national security history. It won’t become apparent until it’s too late.

This analysis has been lost in the discussion, and the NYT failed to ever mention it until now. It is entirely possible that Lutnick reversed a bad trade policy based on sound analysis that it compromises our long-term security. It is also possible that he and the members of the Trump administration engaged in insider trading based on what they knew. Both can be true without making the semiconductor industry, one of the few industries in which the U.S. leads the world and is the envy of the world, a cesspool of Sinophobic spy stories and accusations of treason.

In Doynes article, she states "Rooting for and encouraging others allows us to practice positive empathy, which means feeling some of the same joy that is felt by the person you’re supporting." Although I agree with Doyne, I feel that rooting for yourself and motivating yourself is another crucial way to bring yourself joy. For example, since the beginning of the year, whenever I drive my sisters I school the second we pull into the schools parking lot my sister plays "There She Go's" by The La's. This is one simple way that my sisters and I remind ourselves that we got this in the morning and are capable of taking on the day. comments.name: Georgie
comments.body: When I’m feeling down and seeking joy, I will usually sit with my dogs because when I greet them, they wiggle and jump at me, it impossible not to laugh. A memory that makes me happy was when my old dog, Emmy, was still alive. I remember lying across the top of the couch, and she was across from me. She started to howl at a squirrel outside, and started to howl, I howled back; she seemed shocked, rolling off the couch. Thinking about it now, I smile because it was a simple moment of connection between me and my dog. I feel like sometimes people underestimate the bond a pet has with their owner.  Bringing happiness to others does bring me joy because seeing someone's face light up even at the smallest of compliments probably means a lot to them; I know it does to me, and I’d want someone to do the same for me. I have experienced collective effervescence quite recently at a Giant Rooks concert.  The people in the crowd were jumping up and down and cheering while the band was having fun making music together. It made me feel energized and excited. I think cultivating joy is one of the most important things a person can do. It gives you drive, helps strengthen your relationships, and just feels nice. I think that Dr. McGonigal is right when she says, “As you go about your day, Dr. McGonigal said, make a point of noticing “micro-uplifts,”” I think that even the smallest doses of joy can improve your overall life and its important to seek.

Alongside my school day, I frequently find that playing the piano and cello can improve my mood. 

Dr. Kelly McGonigal points out in her blog that ‘these really small moments don’t have to fix everything to matter.’ I completely agree with this. Usually people would not need to take large amounts of time from their daily lives to improve their wellbeing. Successfully performing a small difficult bar of music within an orchestra and even running around a track can all act as ‘micro-uplifts’ and provide a quick increase in energy for me.

I am also very fond of the term ‘collective effervescence’. Whether it is working togetther within a string quartet or being in a team within a robotics competition, it is useful to know that our good emotions are intensified by sharing them with others.

comments.name: Justin Stanley
comments.body: For me one of the biggest ways I bring joy to my life is by playing basketball and spending quality time with my friends and family. Basketball gives me excitement and something to look forward to especially when I have had a long or stressful day. Being around my teammates in the gym or just having fun competing in drills always put me in a better mood. One of my favorite memories is celebrating the win we got last year against Haverford Everyone doubts us and we succeed in getting a big win. In the article, Dr. McGonigal says, “These really small moments don’t have to fix everything to matter.” I agree with this because sometimes the little things, like laughing with friends, listening to music, or having a good practice, can make someone's day ten times better. In addition I also think by making someone else's day better it can bring joy to yourself because it feels good knowing you did a good thing. It's very important to find joy in everyday life instead of waiting for big moments.

comments.body: One thing that I do to keep a positive mood is to keep my surroundings clean, and uncluttered. I feel like the more clutter is around me the more scrambled my head feels and that is what causes a bad mood. There are little things that also help me derive mood up, like fixing something that has been at a slight offset, or maybe cleaning up something that I have been meaning to clean for a while. Those little victories can help a lot, even if they feel completely useless.

comments.body: Ah, a wonderful life of riches, high class, exquisite designs,  fashion to the nth degree, gorgeous models, patrons like Richard Burton/Elizabeth Taylor, and Italy at its best . . . such style, my condolences to Paolo's family.  I remember well walking down the Spanish Steps in Rome back in 1982, and down the byways was a Bulgari store. As, America's Edgar Allen Poe aptly wrote in his immortal poem "To Helen:" "On desperate seas long wont to roam, Thy hyacinth hair, thy classic face, Thy Naiad airs have brought me home, To the glory that was Greece, And the grandeur that a was Rome."

comments.name: Steve in Italy
comments.body:
I listened to the obituary. One might think that the NYT would get its automated voice to pronounce the name Bulgari correctly. Is that so difficult?

The accent is on the first syllable, not the second.

If you want to hear a worse one listen to the obit of Stanley Zabar. At least 30 times I had to listen to the short a in the first syllable and the accent was on the second. 

For those of us who are visibly impaired it is a joy to be able to listen to articles. However, the NYT should do things correctly.

comments.name: Roz Chast
comments.body: One story I heard throughout my childhood was that because of my mother’s advanced age (42) and previous abdominal surgeries, the doctors did not want my mother to carry me to term. They thought it would be safer for her that I be born at eight months, at which time I would be removed from her body via Cesarian section. However, that meant that my birthday would fall right on Thanksgiving. So she had a choice: schedule the birth for the day before, or the day after. She told me that she chose the day after, because that would give me one more day to “cook.” Just like a turkey, except without the pop-up button. This is a very unpleasant train of thought, so I think I’ll stop right here.

More and more transitions such as this will be necessary if we ever get serious about climate change.
Or are forced to after we’ve suffered enough.

comments.name: Fabrice
comments.body:
This is an important human story, and there are more like these to tell. Missing however is that just three days ago governments failed to agree on a text for COP31 because Europe and many others would not accept a text that did not mention the need to phase out fossil fuels. 

Thus two things struck me in this article. The first is the failure to mention coal and its impact on climate change. Second, that the framing seems to question our moral imperative to keep such a mine open; whereas the ravaging impact of climate change would emphasize our need to do so. 

Where I wish the article would have gone further, was reporting this very human story with greater attention to what our obligations are to these men and their families in supporting a transition to alternative livelihoods.
